newsitem.title: CHILE: Chileans vote in local polls, seen backing Frei.
newsitem.headline: Chileans vote in local polls, seen backing Frei.

text.p: Chileans voted on Sunday in the country's first-ever direct mayoral elections, with polls showing President Eduardo Frei's centre-left coalition headed for an overwhelming victory.
Polling stations were calm and under military guard as eight million voters across the nation cast ballots, including former dictator General Augusto Pinochet who voted early at a Santiago school.

Even the government's opponents say the four parties in Frei's coalition, currently presiding over a vigorous economy and stable politics, will win about 50 percent of the vote combined in the elections for mayors and councillors in Chile's 341 cities and towns.
An alliance of two right-wing parties is expected to finish second with about 30 percent, with the rest split between smaller parties and independents, opinion polls showed.

"The political balance in Chile won't change very much with these elections," said Jovino Novoa, president of the conservative Independent Democratic Union (UDI) party. His party's own polls suggest Frei's coalition, known as La Concertacion, will carry about 50 percent of the vote.

The elections mark the first time Chileans choose their mayors directly under reforms enacted after the last municipal polls in 1992, a change analysts say will benefit figures with high name recognition like Santiago Mayor Jaime Ravinet.
Under the former system, Chileans elected councillors who then elected the mayor, except during the Pinochet regime of 1973-1990 when mayors were appointed by the military.
"People will elect figures with well-known names and personalities. That's the reality," said Ravinet, a member of Frei's Christian Democratic Party.

Known for his red hair and elegant tastes, Ravinet is expected to win re-election easily and could use the results to boost his alleged presidential ambitions in general elections in 1999. He has spent heavily on the campaign although he has faced little opposition.
Ravinet recently published a newspaper advertisement with endorsements from top Chilean artists and intellectuals, including novelist Antonio Skarmeta and folk singer Isabel Parra.
Also expected to win re-election easily is the mayor of Santiago suburb Las Condes, Joaquin Lavin, an UDI member and nationally prominent figure on the right.

With coalition parties competing separately in the elections, pollsters say two left-wing groups, the Party for Democracy (PPD) and the Socialists, could benefit at the expense of the Christian Democrats.

If they do, analysts said it would strengthen the position of Public Works Minister Ricardo Lagos of the Party for Democracy over his Christian Democratic rivals for the coalition's 1999 presidential nomination.
Polls show that Lagos, a leading opponent of military rule in the 1980s, is the only politician in Chile more popular than Frei, who cannot seek re-election.
Lagos, for his part, sought to dampen such speculation.
"I don't see any presidential projections in this, and I'm glad there isn't. We're electing mayors and councillors, that's all," he told reporters after voting.
